Day one, after the talk: Imran sat in his car outside the office for twenty minutes. Parveen's words kept replaying: "You used my worst week to look better." His first thought was, She's making me the villain. His second was, She's right.
Day three: He drafted a long message about how much their friendship meant, how sorry he felt, how hard this was for him. He read it back and deleted it. It was all about him.
Day ten: He asked their manager for a meeting and said plainly that what he'd shared about Parveen's leave, when her mother was unwell, was private and unfair to raise, and that he wanted it kept out of her review. His face burned the whole time. Then he wrote to Parveen: "I've corrected what I said to Menon. I'm not asking for anything back."

qa.q: Where did Imran sit after the talk?
qa.a: Imran sat in his car outside the office for twenty minutes.

qa.q: Why did Imran delete the long message on day three?
qa.a: Imran felt ashamed once he saw the message was all about his own feelings, and knew it wouldn't repair anything for Parveen.

qa.q: Which step on day ten counts as real amends?
qa.a: Going to the manager to correct what he said, even with his face burning, repairs actual harm; the note to Parveen asks for nothing back.

qa.q: How might Parveen see Imran's correction to Menon?
qa.a: Parveen may still be hurt, but seeing Imran take a real, costly step could make it possible to trust him a little again.

grounding: Shows a man torn between defence and remorse after being confronted, choosing real amends over sentiment and image.

Sit, Rekha. You asked why Simran aunty and your Harish mama are still friends after thirty years. It wasn't always simple.
When I was twenty-five, we were both up for the same post at the bank. I told our branch manager that Simran had cried in the strongroom over her divorce and "might not be stable". I got the post.
She found out, came to my desk and said, very quietly, "You knew what that week cost me." I felt naked in front of the whole branch. My first instinct was to defend myself, to say everyone does it.
I didn't sleep for days. Then I went to the manager and said I'd been wrong and unfair about her. It cost me some respect. Then I told Simran I wouldn't ask her to forgive me.
It took her two years. Some people protect their name, beta. I'm glad I lost a little of mine.

qa.q: What did Harish tell the branch manager about Simran?
qa.a: Harish told the branch manager that Simran had cried in the strongroom over her divorce and 'might not be stable'.

qa.q: What was Harish feeling when Simran came to his desk?
qa.a: Harish felt exposed, 'naked in front of the whole branch', and torn between defending himself and admitting the wrong.

qa.q: What amends did Harish make, beyond saying sorry?
qa.a: Harish went back to the manager and admitted he had been wrong and unfair, at a cost to his own reputation, and didn't pressure Simran to forgive him.

qa.q: What might those two years have been like for Simran?
qa.a: Simran likely needed time to see whether his change was real, holding both her hurt and the proof that he had corrected the record.

grounding: Illustrates, in an uncle's memory, a man facing the shame of betraying a friend and choosing real amends over protecting his image.

Tuesday. Hansa confronted Ojas in the office pantry: "You told Ravi about my divorce so he'd look at you for the promotion." Ojas said, "That's not how it happened," and felt his face burn. He went home and told himself she was being dramatic.

Saturday, four days later. He couldn't sleep. He kept seeing Hansa's face. He opened a message to her and typed, "I'm sorry you feel..." then deleted it. It sounded like protecting himself. He sat on the balcony until three, torn between defending himself and admitting it.

Monday, the next week. He asked Hansa for ten minutes. "I did it. I told Ravi because I was scared he'd pick you. It was wrong. I'm going to tell him myself that it wasn't my story to share." She didn't smile. But she said, "Okay. Do that first."

qa.q: Where did Hansa confront Ojas?
qa.a: In the office pantry.

qa.q: What was Ojas feeling on the balcony until three?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and torn between defending himself and admitting what he did, unable to sleep.

qa.q: What makes Ojas's final apology more than sentiment?
qa.a: He admits exactly what he did and why, and commits to a real action, telling Ravi himself that it wasn't his story to share.

qa.q: How might Hansa see his apology?
qa.a: She is still hurt and cautious, but sees a real chance for the friendship if he actually follows through with Ravi.

grounding: Over several days Ojas moves from defending himself to staying with his shame and making real amends, giving the friendship a chance.

passage:
Elizabeth, you asked how I lost my best friend. Your Chinmay uncle has a story he doesn't like telling.

When I was your age, I told our manager that my friend Surya had been secretly interviewing elsewhere. I wanted his project. When Surya found out, he came to my desk and asked, "Why?"

I felt naked. And I did the worst thing: I protected my image. I said I'd only mentioned it because I was worried about him. I even believed it for a while.

Surya looked at me for a long moment and walked away. We never spoke again.

Years later, I saw another colleague in the same spot. She admitted it, apologised to the whole team, and asked to be taken off the project she'd gained. Her friend forgave her slowly.

That's the choice, beta. Face the shame, or protect the image and lose the friend.

qa.q: What did Chinmay tell the manager about Surya?
qa.a: That Surya had been secretly interviewing elsewhere.

qa.q: How did Chinmay feel when Surya asked "Why?"
qa.a: He felt exposed, "naked", and ashamed, and chose to protect his image instead of admitting the truth.

qa.q: What choice in the story could have saved the friendship?
qa.a: Admitting what he did to Surya and making real amends, as the later colleague did by apologising and giving up the project.

qa.q: What was it like for Surya when Chinmay claimed to be worried about him?
qa.a: Surya probably felt betrayed a second time and saw that Chinmay was protecting himself, so he walked away.

grounding: Chinmay uncle recalls protecting his image instead of facing his shame after betraying a friend, and losing the friendship, contrasted with a colleague who made real amends.

passage:
Akash had until 9 a.m. on Monday, when the partner would announce the new project lead, to decide what to do.

On Friday, Pallavi had found out that he'd told the partner about her mistakes on the Mehra account, mistakes she had confided to him as a friend, to make himself look better. She hadn't shouted. She had just said, "I thought you were the one person I didn't have to be careful with."

All weekend he swung between two stories. In one, he had only been honest about the work. In the other, he had used his friend's trust to get ahead. His cheeks burned every time he let the second one in.

On Sunday night he wrote to the partner: "I shared information Pallavi told me in confidence, and I did it to make myself look better. I'd like to withdraw from consideration for the lead."

Then he called Pallavi. "I told him. I'm sorry. I know it doesn't fix it."

qa.q: What time was the partner going to announce the new project lead?
qa.a: 9 a.m. on Monday.

qa.q: What do Akash's burning cheeks show about his feelings?
qa.a: They show he feels ashamed and exposed, torn between defending himself and admitting he used Pallavi's trust.

qa.q: Why does withdrawing from consideration count as real amends?
qa.a: It gives up the gain he got from the betrayal and tells the partner the truth, which is more than just saying sorry.

qa.q: How might Pallavi feel when Akash calls to say he told the partner?
qa.a: She may still be hurt but surprised and a little reassured that he chose honesty over protecting his image.

grounding: Facing a deadline, Akash stays with his shame and makes real amends by admitting the betrayal and withdrawing from the promotion.

Rekha had gone silent after Jeevan told their boss about her plan to resign, and now, two weeks later, she'd agreed to meet him at the tea stall outside the Andheri station.

Jeevan had rehearsed two speeches on the train. One began, "Look, I was under a lot of pressure." The other began, "I was wrong."

When Rekha sat down, looking tired and guarded, the first speech came into his mouth. He felt hot, exposed, like everyone at the stall could see.

He swallowed it.

"I told Kapoor because I wanted him to see me as loyal. It cost you your bonus. I'm ashamed of it." He pushed an envelope across. "I've written to Kapoor saying I misrepresented what you said. This is a copy."

Rekha read it slowly. She didn't forgive him. But she didn't leave, either.

qa.q: Where did Rekha agree to meet Jeevan?
qa.a: At the tea stall outside the Andheri station.

qa.q: What was Jeevan feeling when the first speech came into his mouth?
qa.a: He felt hot and exposed, torn between defending himself and owning his shame.

qa.q: Why does the letter to Kapoor matter more than just saying sorry?
qa.a: It is a real amend that corrects the damage, showing Jeevan is willing to face consequences, not just protect his image.

qa.q: How might Rekha be feeling as she reads the letter?
qa.a: Rekha is guarded and still hurt, but the letter may give her a first reason to consider whether trust can return.

grounding: A man who betrayed a colleague feels exposed and torn, then chooses remorse and a real amend over defending his image.
